Holidays and family

Christmas with an Alcoholic: How to Get Through the Holidays

Over the holidays, drinking becomes almost invisible. A sober alcoholic explains from the inside why, and what you can do before, during and after.

Steven H. White · approximately 9 min read

“Not what he or she is going to do. You can’t decide that. What you want.”

This article shares personal experience and general information. It is not a substitute for medical, psychological, or addiction care.

Everyone has a picture of Christmas. Lights, warmth, the family together, laughter at the table. And there’s another picture we talk about less often: the tense waiting to see what today will be like. Which glass will change the tone of his voice. When you’ll have to come up with another story for the relatives.

If you know that second picture, this article is for you. Not to tell you how to make the holidays perfect. But to make it a little easier to get through them.

Why are the holidays harder?

The rest of the year, drinking has limits: work, early mornings, everyday life. Over the holidays, those limits disappear. People are off work, there are guests everywhere, and most importantly: at Christmas, everyone drinks. Suddenly drinking is normal. A glass of champagne, a bit of mulled wine, a toast with the relatives. For someone who is dependent, that isn’t a challenge. It’s cover.

My Christmases

In my family, it was normal for everyone to drink at the holidays. As a child, that was just how things were, and later, when I was drinking myself, I wasn’t looking forward to the good food. I was looking forward to finally being allowed to drink all day.

As time went on, my drinking was already causing damage, in words and in actions. The pressure came from every direction. The holidays became my “legal” drinking: at Christmas nobody confronted me the same way, there was less conflict, I could let loose, and everyone took it for granted. That’s why I looked forward to it so much.

In my twenties, my two friends, my girlfriend at the time and I decided to go to midnight mass. And we did go. Before that, while we were chatting and getting ready, we put away two bottles of hard liquor between us. For us, that was normal.

Later, as a married man, Christmas meant presents, drinking and TV, if we didn’t go anywhere. Most of the time, the all-day preparations, which mostly meant moving the tree back and forth, had already delivered the “right” amount.

When my family noticed, I don’t know. I think it was already in my teens, but back then it could still be blamed on something: it’s the holidays, he’s a teenager, he’s young. When it turned into a problem, I’ll never know. For me it didn’t seem like a problem at the time, but when I look back at the people around me today, I can see that for them it was. And I always had an explanation.

“Christmas, the season of love” was, for me, a hypocritical lie. The real driving force had been alcohol for a long time.

On top of that, the holidays come with expectations. It should be lovely, it should be good, let’s not ruin it. Which means that whoever lives with the person who drinks carries even more: the baking, the presents, the guests, and on top of that, making sure nobody notices what’s really going on.

Before: two or three weeks ahead

Decide what you want. Not what he or she is going to do. You can’t decide that. What you want. A quiet evening with the kids? Not having to carry everything alone? One day when you don’t have to be on watch? If you know what you want, it’s easier to protect it.

Let go of the perfect holiday. The bigger the expectation, the bigger the disappointment. A simpler holiday, with fewer plans and fewer guests, is often far more bearable. It doesn’t have to be the way it was last year, and it doesn’t have to be the way other people do it.

Make your own plan.

1. Your own way home. If you’re visiting relatives, make sure you can leave when you want, and that who drives doesn’t depend on the state he’s in.

2. An ally. A sibling, friend or relative who knows what’s going on and who you can message when it gets hard.

3. A plan for the kids. Where they can go if the mood changes, and who will look after them if you need to leave.

4. One sentence you can say. For example: “I’m taking the kids home now.” Planned in advance, it’s much easier to say out loud.

During the holidays

Don’t argue with someone who’s been drinking. This is one of the most important things. Someone who’s been drinking can’t think clearly, and an argument started in that moment almost always ends worse than it began. Whatever needs to be said can wait for a sober moment.

You don’t have to put on a show. Many people spend the holidays covering up what’s happening in front of the relatives. Making excuses, explaining, taking over his tasks. You don’t have to tell everyone everything, but you don’t have to hide it at any cost either. If someone asks, this is enough: “Yes, it’s a difficult time right now.”

Take breaks. A walk with the dog, a phone call, ten minutes alone in the bathroom. Not running away, just catching your breath. Nobody can get through an entire day of nonstop tense alertness.

If your family member is sober or trying to stop

The holidays can be hard even when your family member isn’t drinking. There’s alcohol everywhere, and everyone keeps offering it. It helps a lot if there are good alcohol-free drinks on the table, and if the family doesn’t turn their sobriety into a topic of conversation. But their sobriety is their responsibility. Guarding the bottles is not your job.

After: the days after the holidays

After the holidays, many people wake up exhausted and disappointed. That’s natural. Don’t decide about your whole relationship on December 27th, when you’re at your most tired. But don’t brush aside what you saw and felt either. Write it down. A month from now, with a calmer head, it will matter.

In January, many people try a month without alcohol, Dry January. If your partner is planning to as well, it can be a good start. Pay attention to how easy it is for them, and what that month reveals. But don’t let your peace of mind depend on whether they make it.

A few questions for yourself

What do I want from these holidays, regardless of what he does?

What did I do last year that I don’t want to do this year?

Who can I message if it gets hard?

How will I get home if I want to leave?

If you are afraid

If the drinking turns into aggression over the holidays, if you’re afraid, or if you feel that you or your children are in danger, don’t stay. Leave, and call your local emergency number (112 in Europe, 999 in the UK, 911 in the US). No holiday is worth putting yourself in danger.

Steven H. White - sober for ten years. These days he celebrates sober.

Have a plan of your own

Your own way home. An ally. A plan for the kids. One sentence you can say when it is time to leave.

One thing to remember

No holiday is worth putting yourself in danger.

You do not have to make the holidays perfect. You are allowed to protect yourself and your children.
